title: En la continue
body: “Continuë” meant continuation or perseverance; here, “in the long run.” Cotgrave’s 1611 dictionary records the noun under continuë (facsimile p. 232).

refs.label: Cotgrave, continuë, facsimile page 232

title: Doctor Gratian
body: Doctor Gratian is the Dottore, a comic doctor in early commedia dell’arte. Desportes’s “played his part” suggests this stock character; the person behind his nickname is unestablished.
cipher: The seven signs permit GRATIAN; the title, print and theatrical wording select that reading.

refs.label: Buckley, Eloquent Action (2009), fig. A30, p. 307
Buckley, p. 312, note 20: the Dottore’s names

images.name: doctor-gratian.png
images.caption: The DOCTOR GRATIAN label in the Recueil Fossard print, reproduced in Buckley, fig. A30.

title: Names behind the words
body: “Our uncle,” the man at the college, and the man of La Chesne are readable designations. The letter does not identify their bearers.
en: our uncle|(?:the )?man (?:of La Chesne|at the college)|friend at the college

refs.label: Frachetta, f. 189

title: Secondé
body: The passage says the proposal was backed by “our Doctor Gratian.” Modernized French reads secondé.
cipher: The last source sign allows E/R. The historical reading retains that small ending choice.

refs.label: Frachetta, f. 189, lines 5–6 and 9

title: DAU DAUTRES → d’autres
body: The source repeats the beginning: DAU DAUTRES. The first DAU is omitted editorially as a likely false start or copying repetition. Its ink is intact and is not crossed out in the manuscript.

refs.label: BnF, français 3984, f. 189 · line 9

images.name: word-dau-repetition.png
images.caption: The two DAU groups, followed by TRES. The first is omitted from the reading.

title: Comme un aveugle des couleurs
body: “Like a blind man discussing colours”: someone speaks confidently about what he cannot know. Desportes writes this proverb in ordinary handwriting amid the cipher.
en: like a blind man speaking of colours

refs.label: Frachetta, f. 189, line 11

title: Particulier
body: Here particulier means “specific”; particulière describes a private quarrel. The companion cipher and its contemporary decipherment supply the written-out word.
cipher: A compact abbreviation represents several letters; it is not a row of separate alphabet signs.

refs.label: Cipher comparison, f. 176v
Contemporary decipherment, f. 177v

title: Poquinteste
body: The name is written twice in a readable companion letter. Those occurrences support this spelling; the person’s precise identity remains unestablished.

refs.label: Companion letter, f. 188

title: Extravagantes
body: “Extravagant” could mean wild, unreasonable or off the point. Cotgrave’s 1611 entry explains the period sense.
cipher: The source spells EXTRAUASANTES. The edition’s [g] corrects the written S; the key itself has not changed.

refs.label: Cotgrave, extravagant, column 421l

title: Quand / quant à
body: The same word-sign serves “even if” and “as for.” Henry IV’s letters provide contemporary parallels for both constructions (printed pp. 125 and 285).
cipher: The arrow represents the word; it cannot determine whether its writer would spell the ending D or T.
en: Even had I|As for your pension|indeed be deprived

refs.label: Henry IV, printed p. 125
Henry IV, printed p. 285

title: Pour récompense
body: “Pour récompense” means “in return” or “as a reward.” Nicot’s 1606 Bonté entry uses the same article-free expression: “qui ne fait rien pour recompense.”
cipher: The horizontal ink cancels material, including an L/Y sign. The running text leaves that cancellation out; c[e qui] remains a disclosed supply.

refs.label: Nicot, Thresor (1606), Bonté
Frachetta, lines 20 and 29

title: Pension · pièce
body: The pension depends on a prelate and a “pièce,” understood here as an item of revenue. The exact benefice and payment arrangement are not named.

refs.label: Frachetta, lines 23–25
Nicot, assister, 1606

title: Tant que
body: Here “tant que” introduces a result: “so much so that.” In Gargantua XIX (1534), laughter becomes so intense “tant que les larmes leurs venoyent es yeulx”—tears come to their eyes.

refs.label: Rabelais, Gargantua, XIX, p. [66] · CESR/Renom transcription

title: [Gondi]
body: Girolamo Gondi is the strong contextual identification for the disastrous journey. Contemporary letters connect his mission with Henry IV’s conversion; this particular code has not been independently assigned the name.
cipher: The three-upright sign remains an unproved designation. Brackets preserve that distinction.

refs.label: Henry IV, 26 April 1593, III, pp. 763–764
Henry IV, 30 May 1593, III, pp. 782–783

images.name: gondi-context.png
images.caption: The three-upright sign after LE VOIAGE DE.

title: Écus · 500,000
body: An écu was a historical French coin and monetary denomination. The letter gives five hundred thousand écus; it does not specify the exact transaction.
cipher: 5 with a raised c means five hundreds; MIL supplies ×1,000. The accepted amount is 500,000.

refs.label: TLFi / CNRTL, écu², sense A
Archives de Meurthe-et-Moselle, historical numerical notation

images.name: amount.png
images.caption: The manuscript’s raised-c quantity before MIL ESCUS.

title: Le légat
body: A legate is the Pope’s representative. Here the title refers to Filippo Sega, Cardinal of Piacenza; his correspondence fits the letter’s July 1593 setting.
cipher: The g-like code aligns with “le légat” in a cipher and its contemporary decipherment; it is not a personal initial.

refs.label: Related cipher, f. 176v
Contemporary decipherment, f. 177v

title: 22 July 1593
body: A contemporary abstract names both Desportes letters and dates them 22 July 1593. The edition writes [22] because the documentary date is clearer than the handwritten numeral.

refs.label: Contemporary abstract, f. 141v, entries 13–14

images.name: date-aldobrandini.png
images.caption: Entry 13 names the Aldobrandini letter and dates it 22 July 1593.

title: The farewell
body: “Vostre humble serviteur”: “your humble servant.” Comparison with the related Lisieux letter supports the formula; the separate paraph has no alphabetic expansion.
cipher: Joined courtesy formulas and contractions are expanded as groups.

refs.label: Frachetta closing
Aldobrandini closing

title: The legate’s nephew
body: The nephew is Girolamo Agucchi (also Agocchi), identified through the British Library correspondence catalogue and an April 1593 signed letter. Malvoisie is plausibly Innocenzo Malvasia; Mateouci / Mateuci is plausibly Girolamo Matteucci.

refs.label: British Library, Add MS 6875, especially items 31, 34–36
Agocchi, 4 April 1593, fr. 3613 f. 69v

title: Pape Grégoire
body: The passage contrasts papal spending during Gregory’s pontificate with the subsequent lack of help. “Pape” is established by earlier manuscripts that write the word above the same sign.
cipher: Three glossed occurrences in two earlier letters identify the lambda-like sign as PAPE.

refs.label: Strongest gloss: fr. 3982, f. 125r, canvas 258
Second gloss: f. 124r, canvas 256

images.name: pape-comparison.png
images.caption: The target and earlier manuscript occurrences carrying a PAPE gloss.

title: L’Infante
body: Infanta is a title for a daughter of the Spanish royal house. Here Desportes recalls a proposal to marry her to one of the French princes.

refs.label: Aldobrandini recto, lines 33–35
Académie française, infante

title: Qui me fit…
body: Older French can use qui to resume a preceding fact, like modern ce qui. Montaigne I.42, p. 261, describes actors returning to humble lives: “qui est leur nayfve et originelle condition.”
en: That made me reject|should not be in a position

refs.label: Montaigne, Essais I.42, displayed p. 261
Montaigne, Essais I.1, displayed p. 8

title: Chacun
body: The surviving AQU(N) and the sentence establish chaqun, modern chacun. The damaged initial [ch] is supplied, and the word continues across the line break.

refs.label: Aldobrandini verso, lines 1–2

title: Bafoué
body: “Bafoué” means mocked or derided. Montaigne, Essais II.12, p. 450, uses the same participle: “Nous n’aurons jamais assez bafoué l’impudence de cet accouplage.”
cipher: A human visual observation led back to the H/U sign: BAF / OUE across two lines, with no supplied letter.

refs.label: Montaigne, Essais II.12, displayed p. 450, ARTFL transcription

images.name: bafoue-comparison.png
images.caption: The disputed sign alongside H/U and E/R controls from the manuscript.

title: Huit tant de papier
body: “Huit tant” means eight times as much. Desportes says a fuller account would fill eight times the paper.

refs.label: Aldobrandini verso, line 17

title: Faucetés
body: Faucetés is the older spelling of faussetés: falsehoods. The word runs FA / UCETES across two lines.
cipher: The extra E/R sign before the word is intact but surplus. It remains visible in the manuscript and is omitted from the reading.

refs.label: Aldobrandini verso, lines 8–9

title: Ont, font
body: The sentence lists what the recipient would know: what their friends have, do, and how weak they are. Montaigne I.50 offers a parallel for adjacent verbs sharing one subject; punctuation is editorial.

refs.label: Montaigne, Essais I.50, De Democritus et Heraclitus

title: Monsieur Guise
body: The letter says Mayenne was willing to accept Guise as king, provided there was a way to defend him. The condition belongs to the proposal; it does not prove that such protection was available.

refs.label: Aldobrandini verso, lines 21–24

title: The closing argument
body: Desportes proposes passing the Pope’s intentions to Mayenne without the legate as intermediary. The English takes the legate as the man acting at Mayenne’s expense; that pronoun assignment is contextual.

refs.label: Aldobrandini verso, lines 25–33

title: V. S. I.
body: “Vostre Seigneurie Illustrissime”: “Your Most Illustrious Lordship,” the courtesy used for Aldobrandini. The letters abbreviate the title in several forms.

refs.label: Aldobrandini manuscript, f. 186

title: Le Saint-Siège
body: The Holy See means the papacy and its authority. “Sa Sainteté” is the Pope’s courtesy title.

refs.label: TLFi / CNRTL, siège, “Saint-Siège”

title: The edition
body: Brackets mark supplied letters or expanded contractions. French modernizes the spelling; English interprets the wording. The manuscript remains the record of the ink.

title: Nostre → Notre
body: The older spelling of notre: “our.”

title: estoit → était
body: “Was”: the third-person singular imperfect of être. The older -oit ending becomes -ait, and initial es- becomes é-.

title: asses → assez
body: The accepted source reading is A–S–S–E–S, with a final S. Assez is the modern spelling: “enough” or “sufficiently.”

refs.label: Académie française, assez · sufficiently / enough

refs.label: Académie française · older -ois and modern -ais

title: cheute → chute
body: Modern chute drops e after h: ‘fall’.

title: seust → sût
body: Modern sût, the third-person singular imperfect subjunctive of savoir (“knew”).

title: auanture → aventure
body: Modern aventure writes v for u and e in place of the following a. Par aventure means ‘perhaps’.

title: mesme → même
body: Modern spelling drops the older s and uses ê.

refs.label: Académie française, 1740 preface · changes in spelling

title: par dela → par-delà
body: Modern par-delà joins the words with a hyphen and accents à: ‘over there’.

title: S[ainc]t siege → Saint-Siège
body: Modern Saint-Siège drops c from sainct, accents è and joins the title with a hyphen. Brackets retain the existing editorial expansions or supplies.

title: du dit → dudit
body: Modern dudit joins du and dit: ‘of the said’ or ‘of the aforementioned’.

title: mal aisé → malaisé
body: Modern malaisé joins the two words: ‘difficult’.

title: soy mesme → soi-même
body: Modern soi-même changes y to i, replaces s with a circumflex and joins the words with a hyphen.

title: roy d’Espagne → roi d’Espagne
body: Modern roi writes i for final y: ‘king of Spain’. The source sign represents the whole title. This spelling belongs to the expanded reading; the source uses a whole-word sign or abbreviation.

title: l aloit → l’allait
body: Modern l’allait adds an apostrophe, doubles l in allait and changes -oit to -ait.

title: n asarderion[s] → n’hasarderion[s]
body: The French view adds h in hasarder and an apostrophe after n. These are editorial changes; the bracketed s remains supplied. Brackets retain the existing editorial expansions or supplies.

title: d autres → d’autres
body: Modern d’autres joins elided de to autres with an apostrophe: ‘other’ here.

title: d elle → d’elle
body: Modern d’elle joins elided de to elle with an apostrophe: here ‘from His Holiness’, agreeing with feminine Sainteté.

title: n en → n’en
body: Modern n’en joins the negative n’ to en with an apostrophe.

title: l on → l’on
body: Modern l’on joins l’ and on with an apostrophe: ‘one’ or an impersonal subject.

title: l advenir → l’avenir
body: Modern l’avenir adds an apostrophe and drops d in advenir: ‘the future’.

title: n user → n’user
body: Modern n’user adds the apostrophe after the negative n’.

title: s i → s’y
body: Modern s’y adds an apostrophe and writes the pronoun y in place of i.

title: n y → n’y
body: Modern n’y joins the negative n’ to the pronoun y with an apostrophe.

title: seroit il → serait-il
body: Modern serait-il changes -oit to -ait and adds the inversion hyphen: ‘would he be’.

title: font ilz → font-ils
body: Modern font-ils changes ilz to ils and adds the inversion hyphen: ‘do they’.

title: en apres → après
body: Here en après means ‘afterwards’. The French view omits en and adds è; this is editorial simplification as well as spelling.

title: l estat → l’État
body: Modern l’État adds the apostrophe, drops s after e and accents É: ‘the state’.

title: nia → n’y a
body: Here n’y a is divided into the negative n’, the pronoun y and the verb a. The source writes i for y.

title: iusques a → jusqu’à
body: Modern jusqu’à elides the ending of jusques, writes j for i and accents à.

title: trouueres uous → trouverez-vous
body: Modern trouverez-vous writes consonantal u as v, changes the vous ending -es to -ez and adds the inversion hyphen.

title: lors que → lorsque
body: Modern lorsque is written as one word: ‘when’. The French view retains the older separation, recorded in the Académie’s 1694 dictionary.

refs.label: Académie française, 1694 · Lors que, vol. 1, p. 664

title: lors quilz → lorsqu’ils
body: Modern lorsqu’ils joins lors and qu’, and changes ilz to ils: ‘when they’. The French view retains lors qu’ils.

refs.label: Académie française, 1694 · Lors que, vol. 1, p. 664

title: suplie → supplie
body: Modern supplie doubles p: ‘beseech’ or ‘implore’.

title: tres → très
body: Modern spelling adds the diacritic: e → è. The word is unchanged.

title: Createur → Créateur
body: Modern spelling adds the diacritic: e → é. The word is unchanged.

title: obeissant → obéissant
body: Modern spelling adds the diacritic: e → é. The word is unchanged.
